source.title: Predicting vs. Acting: A Trade-off Between World Modeling & Agent Modeling
source.authors: Margaret Li; Weijia Shi; Artidoro Pagnoni; Peter West; Ari Holtzman

page_placements.theme: Post-training (RLHF, instruction tuning) and commitment to a response-level plan

record.tranche_reason: The study probes hidden states for tokens several positions in the future, using linear-probe accuracy rather than the rhyme-word interventions in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports perplexity, probability concentration, n-gram overlap, and anchor-span results. The future-token probe results bear directly on V2. Repeated n-grams and anchor spans describe generation patterns, but do not test whether a future-token representation causally changes intermediate text; they are recorded as findings outside the listed versions.
record.test_reason: §4.1 uses the Future Lens method (Pal et al., 2023): a linear probe on one hidden state (layer 28 of Llama 2 7B Base and RLHF) predicts tokens 1–3 steps beyond the next token. Its results bear directly on V2. The rest of the paper (perplexity, probability concentration, n-gram reuse, anchor spans) measures generation patterns, not internal look-ahead, so it fits no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right, but incomplete. The main conclusion is a world-modeling vs agent-modeling trade-off: RLHF models are worse next-token predictors and concentrate probability on a self-predictable subdistribution. RLHF hidden states hold more linearly decodable future-token information on their own generations. Recurring anchor spans act as implicit blueprints for long-form generation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses linear probing of hidden states for future-token prediction, following the methodology of Future Lens; tests Llama 2 7B Base and RLHF at layer 28, including predictions of model-generated text. It does not use rhyme prompts or causal interventions on candidate ending words.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction target matters: RLHF probes do better on their own generations, while Base models are more effective at predicting RLHF generations than the reverse. The probe study uses only the 28th layer and future offsets n=1, 2, and 3.

fits_no_version.finding: RLHF generations reuse n-grams and ordered anchor spans across samples for the same prompt; Base generations do not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RLHF-adapted models produce repeatable long-form scaffolding (anchor spans) across samples for a prompt, more than Base models.

fits_no_version.finding: RLHF models concentrate next-token probability (top-1 mass near 0.9 on their own generations) and have lower perplexity on their own outputs (§3, Figures 3–5). No rows record this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RLHF models are more self-predictable on their own generations than Base models.

record.problems: The future-token probe results are shown in Figure 6 without numerical values in the text, and the text does not state a chance baseline or uncertainty for those accuracies. Probe tests cover one layer, one model family and offsets only through n=3. The paper notes that it lacks multiple random seeds and broad model coverage.

untested.parts: Offsets beyond 3 steps past the next token; layers other than 28; models outside Llama 2 7B; any chance or bigram baseline for probe accuracy.
Not tested: no rhyme task or intervention.
Not tested: no causal test of features computed for later positions.
Not tested: no reasoning, chess or Sokoban task.
Not tested directly. The authors attribute higher RLHF decodability to more predictable output, but run no test separating planning from local predictability.

missing.what: Numeric probe accuracies and any chance or simple-baseline accuracy for the future-token probes

record.verdict_notes: The probe offsets are counted after the next token, so n=1–3 means roughly 2–4 positions ahead. All probe evidence is figure-only, with no chance baseline or seeds. The authors attribute the RLHF advantage to more predictable outputs, not shown planning; this is relevant to V6 but not a test of it. Future Lens is an original source for V2, but this study is not, so verdicts are allowed.

versions.untested_parts: No rhyming-verse task, candidate rhyme-word representation, or intervention that changes a rhyme ending.
Tests linear decoding at the 28th layer for 1, 2, and 3 future-token offsets on the Pile and Anthropic Helpful datasets; does not establish decodability at farther offsets or across other models.
No causal test of whether a feature is computed for its benefit to later positions rather than as a side effect of next-token prediction.
No open-weight rhyme-planning test or open attribution-graph intervention.
No multi-step reasoning, chess, or Sokoban task.
The study does not test whether the apparent plans are incidental local features or heuristics, or whether intervening on them changes the generated text.

relation.reason: The study reports its own future-token probing results bearing directly on V2.

tranche.reason: §4.1 explicitly follows Pal et al. (2023), using a linear probe on a single hidden representation and future-token prediction accuracy.

source_check.notes: The paper defines n=1–3 relative to the next token being predicted, corresponding to positions t+2 through t+4 from the hidden-state position. Figure-only baselines denote model comparisons, not an established chance baseline; recurring output spans do not establish a causal internal planning mechanism.

statements.correction: §4.2: almost twice as many RLHF sequences share a 10-gram as Base sequences; a quarter of RLHF outputs share a 25-gram. Figure 8: Llama 2 70B RLHF has ordered common anchor spans; Base lacks that structure for the illustrated prompt. §3: RLHF own-generation top-token probability is nearly 0.9; Figure 5 reports lower own-generation perplexity.
statements.problem: Base generations also share n-grams, at lower rates; the absence finding concerns the common anchor structure in Figure 8. Figure 7's text does not identify its models as Llama 2 70B.

reader_labels.reason: Predictive information is asymmetric: Base models are reported as more effective at predicting RLHF generations than the reverse. See probe-pile-cross-base-to-rlhf-1 through probe-helpful-cross-rlhf-to-base-3.
